example.question: Why solids have a fixed volume and shape according to particle theory of matter?

explain.title: Particles are always moving
explain.body: According to this theory, matter is composed of very small particles called molecules which are always in motion. Their motion may be vibrational, rotational or linear. Molecules have kinetic energy due to their motion.

explain.title: Forces act between molecules
explain.body: There exists a mutual force of attraction between the molecules known as intermolecular force. This force depends upon the distance between the molecules. It decreases with increasing distance between them. Molecules also possess potential energy due to this force of attraction.

explain.title: Heating makes molecular motion more vigorous
explain.body: When a substance is heated, its temperature rises and its molecular motion becomes more vigorous which increases the kinetic energy of the molecules. Thus, the temperature of the substance depends upon the average kinetic energy of its molecules.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: In solids, strong intermolecular forces hold molecules at fixed positions, but the molecules vibrate about those positions. Liquids have weaker intermolecular forces, so molecules can slide over one another and the liquid flows. Gas molecules are relatively far away from one another, so a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.

explain.title: Plasma
explain.body: The plasma is a gas in which most of the atoms are ionized containing positive ions and electrons. These particles move freely. Their presence makes plasma a conducting state of matter, which is why plasma is known as the fourth state of matter.

mistakes: Do not say that molecules in a solid are motionless; they vibrate about fixed positions.
Do not say that a liquid has a definite shape. It has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
Do not say that a gas has a definite volume. It has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.
Do not say that intermolecular force increases as molecules get farther apart; it decreases with increasing distance.
Do not describe plasma as an ordinary gas: it contains positive ions and free electrons and conducts electricity.

explain.title: Why a thermometer is needed
explain.body: Our sense of touch can tell us whether something feels hot or cold, but it cannot measure the exact temperature. A thermometer is an instrument used to measure temperature. Thermometers use some property of a substance, which changes appreciably with the change of temperature.

explain.title: Choosing a thermometric material
explain.body: Some basic thermometric properties for a material suitable to construct a thermometer are the following: It is a good conductor of heat; it gives quick response to temperature changes; it has uniform thermal expansion; it has high boiling point; it has low freezing point; it has large expansivity (low specific heat capacity); it does not wet glass; it does not vapourize; it is visible.

explain.title: Liquid-in-glass thermometers
explain.body: Liquids expand on heating, so the expansion in the volume of a liquid can be used to measure temperature. A liquid-in-glass thermometer has a glass bulb filled with liquid and a narrow capillary tube. As the temperature rises, the liquid expands and moves up the tube. The position of the end of the liquid thread gives the temperature. Mercury is opaque and easy to see; alcohol must be coloured to make it visible.

explain.title: Fixed points and temperature scales
explain.body: A temperature scale is constructed using two reference temperatures called fixed points. The steam point is the upper fixed point and the melting point of pure ice is the lower fixed point. Celsius assigns 0 and 100 to these points; Fahrenheit assigns 32 and 212; Kelvin assigns 273 and 373. Kelvin is also called the absolute temperature scale.

explain.title: Converting temperatures
explain.body: For Celsius to Fahrenheit use T_f = 9/5 × T_c + 32. For Fahrenheit to Celsius use T_c = 5/9 (T_f − 32). For Celsius to Kelvin use T_k = T_c + 273. Substitute the given value into the appropriate formula and include the correct unit in your answer.

explain.title: Thermocouple thermometers
explain.body: A thermocouple has two wires made of different materials joined to form two junctions. When the junctions are at different temperatures, a small current and potential difference are produced. A greater temperature difference produces a greater potential difference. Thermocouples are useful for very high temperatures and rapidly changing temperatures.

mistakes: Do not confuse the lower fixed point with the upper fixed point: the ice point is lower and the steam point is upper.
Do not use the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit formula when converting Fahrenheit to Celsius; use T_c = 5/9 (T_f − 32).
Do not forget the +273 when converting Celsius to Kelvin, or the temperature unit in the final answer.
Do not say that touch measures exact temperature; it only gives an idea of hotness or coldness.
Do not describe the liquid level as the temperature without explaining that the position of the end of the thread is read against the scale.
For thermometer-length problems, do not treat the length above the lower mark as the full fixed-point interval.

explain.title: Sensitivity
explain.body: Sensitivity of a thermometer refers to its ability to detect small changes in the temperature of an object. For example, a thermometer marked every 0.1°C is more sensitive than one marked every 1°C.

explain.title: Range
explain.body: This refers to the span of temperature, from low to high, over which the thermometer can measure accurately. A clinical thermometer has a short range, about 35°C to 45°C, while a laboratory thermometer may have a longer range.

explain.title: The liquid affects range
explain.body: The choice of liquid for thermometers puts a lower and upper limit for the range of a thermometer. Mercury freezes at −39°C and boils at 357°C; alcohol freezes at about −112°C and boils at 78°C.

explain.title: Linearity
explain.body: This refers to a direct proportional relationship between the temperature and scale reading across entire range of measurement. A good linear thermometer has evenly spaced markings, so equal scale increments correspond to equal temperature changes.

Do not define linearity only as having evenly spaced marks; explain that equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.

When comparing scale divisions, remember that smaller divisions indicate greater sensitivity.

explain.title: Particles in the three states
explain.body: Matter is made of particles. In a solid, particles are closely packed and vibrate about mean positions. In a liquid, particles remain close but can move past one another. In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely in random directions.

explain.title: Temperature and heat
explain.body: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Heat is energy in transit from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature. A body contains internal energy, not heat.

explain.title: Thermometers and their properties
explain.body: A thermometer uses a thermometric property that changes with temperature. Sensitivity describes the change in reading for a temperature change; range is the interval it can measure; linearity means equal temperature changes give equal scale changes.

explain.title: Temperature scales
explain.body: The Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales use different fixed-point readings. For ice and steam points they are 0°C and 100°C, 32°F and 212°F, and approximately 273 K and 373 K. Kelvin starts at absolute zero.

explain.title: Liquid-in-glass thermometers
explain.body: A liquid-in-glass thermometer has a bulb and a narrow graduated capillary. A large bulb and narrow capillary improve sensitivity. A liquid that expands uniformly gives a more linear scale; the liquid’s properties and tube length affect the range.

notes.title: How particles explain the states of matter
notes.answer: Matter consists of very small particles that are always in motion. Their spacing, motion and intermolecular forces explain the properties of its states.
notes.explanation: Matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. The forces between these particles and the way they move help explain the properties of solids, liquids, gases and plasma.
notes.simple: Think of particles as tiny moving pieces. In a solid they stay close to fixed places, in a liquid they slide past one another, and in a gas they are far apart and move freely.
examples: Solid: its particles vibrate about fixed positions, so it has a definite shape and volume.
Gas: its particles are far apart, so it has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
steps: Identify how the particles are arranged and move.
Relate their motion and spacing to the forces between them.
Use these features to explain whether the substance has a definite shape or volume.

notes.title: Temperature, Heat and Internal Energy
notes.answer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference.
notes.explanation: Temperature tells how hot or cold a body is. Heat is energy transferred between bodies because they have different temperatures. A body has internal energy, not heat stored inside it.
notes.simple: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. Heat is energy moving from a hotter object to a colder one.
examples: A spoon becomes hot when left in hotter water: thermal energy transfers from the water to the spoon.
When you touch a cold surface, energy transfers from your warmer hand to the surface.
steps: Compare the temperatures of the two bodies.
Thermal energy transfers from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.
The energy transferred is called heat.
The sum of the molecules' kinetic and potential energies is the body's internal energy.
notes.checkQuestion: Which way does thermal energy flow when two bodies have different temperatures?
notes.checkAnswer: Thermal energy flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.

notes.title: Thermometers and temperature scales
notes.answer: A thermometer measures temperature using a thermometric property that changes with temperature.
notes.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature by using a property that changes when temperature changes. Temperature scales use fixed points, and the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin readings are related by formulae.
notes.simple: A thermometer uses a measurable change, such as the expansion of mercury, to show temperature. Use the correct formula to convert between temperature scales.

notes.title: Sensitivity, Range and Linearity
notes.answer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes; range is the span of temperatures measured; linearity means equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.
notes.explanation: A thermometer is judged by three features: sensitivity (detecting small temperature changes), range (the temperatures it measures), and linearity (equal temperature changes giving equal scale changes). For example, a thermometer marked every 0.1°C is more sensitive than one marked every 1°C. A clinical thermometer has a short range, while a laboratory thermometer can have a longer range. A linear thermometer has evenly spaced scale markings.
notes.simple: Sensitivity tells how small a change a thermometer can notice. Range tells how low and high a temperature it can measure. Linearity means equal temperature changes produce equal scale changes.
examples: A thermometer with 0.1°C divisions is more sensitive than one with 1°C divisions.
A thermometer with evenly spaced scale markings shows linearity.
steps: Check the smallest scale division to compare sensitivity: smaller divisions allow smaller changes to be detected.
Find the lowest and highest temperatures marked to identify the range.
Check whether equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale intervals to identify linearity.
notes.checkQuestion: What does sensitivity tell us about a thermometer?
notes.checkAnswer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes.

notes.title: How a Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer Works
notes.answer: The thin bulb wall helps the liquid respond quickly to temperature changes, while the narrow, uniform bore makes its expansion readable on a linear scale.
notes.explanation: A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because its liquid expands when heated and moves up a narrow, uniform tube. The bulb transfers heat to the liquid; the tube and liquid together make the temperature readable on a scale.
notes.simple: Heat makes the liquid in the bulb expand. It rises in the thin tube, and the scale shows the temperature.
examples: Mercury in a thermometer rises when its temperature increases.
A fine, uniform bore makes a small expansion easier to read on the scale.
steps: The thin wall of the glass bulb allows quick conduction through glass to the liquid from a hot object whose temperature is to be measured.
The liquid responds to the change in temperature and expands.
The uniformity of the narrow tube or bore ensures even expansion of the liquid required to make the linear measuring scale.
Read the liquid level against the scale.
notes.checkQuestion: Why should a liquid-in-glass thermometer have a narrow, uniform tube and a thin-walled bulb?
notes.checkAnswer: The narrow, uniform bore makes the liquid’s expansion correspond evenly to the scale; the thin bulb wall helps heat reach the liquid quickly.
